analysis.one_liner: Bans new large factory farms and forces meatpackers to buy more livestock on the open market.
analysis.headline: The Farm System Reform Act never received a committee vote; with 40 Democratic cosponsors but no Republican support, it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would freeze the growth of the largest factory farms, requiring the biggest concentrated animal feeding operations to stop operating as such by 2040, and would create a $10 billion-a-year program to pay off farmers' debts when they transition out of those operations. It would make meat companies jointly liable for pollution and health harms at the farms they contract with, ban packers from owning the livestock they slaughter, require half of each packer's slaughter volume to come from open-market purchases, restrict the poultry 'tournament' pay system, and restore mandatory country-of-origin labels for beef, pork, and dairy. It was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent ranchers, contract poultry and hog growers, and small meat processors gain bargaining power and open-market price discovery. Rural residents living near large factory farms gain new legal remedies for pollution, odor, and health harms. Consumers gain clearer origin labels. Taxpayers and the environment gain from reduced water and air pollution over time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent farmers, rural residents, and consumers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans new or expanded large concentrated animal feeding operations and requires existing large CAFOs to cease operating as large CAFOs by January 1, 2040, with civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation per day.

It creates a voluntary program, funded at $10 billion every year, that grants money to farmers to pay off debts from building a factory farm and to convert the property to pasture-based livestock, specialty crops, or organic production.

It makes meat companies that control contract farms jointly and non-delegably liable for waste disposal, water and air pollution, harm to contract growers and neighbors, and property value losses, and lets any affected person sue with attorney's fees awarded to a prevailing plaintiff.

It amends the 1921 Packers and Stockyards Act to ban most packers from owning or feeding livestock before slaughter, require at least 50 percent of a large packer's slaughter volume to be bought through open spot-market sales, outlaw formula-priced forward contracts without a firm base price, and make it unlawful for poultry companies to pay growers through the tournament system when the comparison uses factors the company controls.

It restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy products, and allows a 'Product of U.S.A.' label only on meat from animals exclusively born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States.

analysis.who_pays: The largest meatpacking companies and poultry integrators (such firms would lose owned-livestock procurement, exclusive contracting practices, and pollution immunity), large factory-farm operators facing the phase-out and penalties, and taxpayers, who fund the $10 billion annual transition program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meatpackers, poultry integrators, large CAFO operators

drawbacks.text: The transition program is expensive: the bill transfers $10 billion from the Treasury every year, indefinitely, to pay off farmers' debts and convert farm properties.

Requiring packers to divest livestock ownership and buy at least half their slaughter volume on the spot market, and to stop using formula-priced contracts, would force a rapid reorganization of meat procurement that could disrupt supply chains and raise procurement costs in the transition years.

The moratorium applies the moment of enactment with penalties of up to $10,000 per day, and the 2040 phase-out applies to operations built before it, so existing large operations have no grandfathering beyond the eventual deadline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: a small number of meatpackers control most cattle and hog slaughter, and contract growers bear debt and pollution risk for companies that control their pay and their birds. The tradeoffs are the $10 billion annual cost of transition grants and the disruption of forcing packers to reorganize procurement quickly. The 2040 phase-out gives existing operations nearly two decades to adjust, and the voluntary debt-forgiveness program is designed to compensate farmers who exit, which softens the blow. On balance the benefits to independent farmers, rural communities, and consumers are large, but the price tag and procurement mandates are serious costs an honest supporter must acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Agriculture and Transportation and Infrastructure committees, referred to two subcommittees, and never got a markup or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Farm System Reform Act of 2021 on July 13, 2021, with 40 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction.
On July 14, 2021 it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, and on August 11, 2021 to the Livestock and Foreign Agriculture Subcommittee.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest meatpackers and poultry integrators kept the contracting structures, packer ownership of livestock, and pollution arrangements the bill would have ended, and large factory farms continued to expand.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where a partisan split could be recorded.

industries.note: The bill bans most packers from owning or feeding livestock before slaughter, requires at least half of slaughter volume to be bought through open spot-market bidding, and outlaws formula-priced forward contracts without a firm base price — directly attacking the procurement methods of the four-firm concentrated packing industry. Its gain is ordinary farmers' loss of bargaining power, so its interest runs against the public's.

The bill makes integrators jointly liable for waste, pollution, and harm to growers and neighbors, subjects live poultry dealers to Packers and Stockyards enforcement and injunction authority, and restricts the tournament pay system that compares growers using inputs the company controls. The industry's profit model depends on shifting risk onto contract growers.

The bill freezes new and expanded large CAFOs at enactment and phases out existing large CAFOs by 2040, with penalties up to $10,000 per day. The pollution and property-value costs these operations impose on neighbors are exactly what the bill makes the controlling companies pay for.

industries.industry: Contract growers and independent livestock farmers
industries.note: Growers gain access to debt-forgiveness grants to exit factory farming, the right to contract data and jury trials, protection from retaliatory termination, and attorney's fees in Packers and Stockyards suits. Their interest runs alongside rural residents' and consumers'.
Taxpayers fund the $10 billion annual transition program without an offset, in exchange for eventual reductions in factory-farm pollution as large CAFOs are phased out.
